title: Big Tech Unites for Open Source AI—and Against Anthropic
dek: Two open-source stories collide: NVIDIA quietly bets on Ilya Sutskever's secretive Safe Superintelligence, while $8 trillion of tech market cap signs an open letter defending open-weight AI — leaving Anthropic standing alone and getting either villain or hero framing depending on where you sit.

oneIdea.headline: Eight trillion dollars of Big Tech just made open-weight AI a coalition — and Anthropic the lone holdout.
oneIdea.summary: As Washington edges toward banning Chinese open models, NVIDIA, Google, Microsoft, Meta, Elon Musk, Palantir and eventually OpenAI co-signed an open letter defending open weights. Read cynically it's everyone talking their book against the two labs running away with the market; read charitably it's a fight against regulatory capture. Either way, Anthropic's refusal to sign turned it into a Rorschach test — villain to some, principled and 'aura-farming' to others — and the messy employee snark on both sides shows just how heated the open-versus-closed war has become.

gpCorner.note: AI commentary for UK general practice; not from the podcast

items.title: Open weights are the only version of this that can ever run inside the NHS
items.body: Strip away the Washington politics and there is a practical point for general practice. An open-weight model is one anyone can download and run on their own infrastructure — which is the only arrangement under which patient-identifiable audio or text never leaves an NHS-controlled environment. Every ambient scribe now in use in English general practice sends the consultation to a supplier's cloud, and the DPIA turns on trusting that supplier's processing terms. If the open ecosystem thrives, on-premise or UK-hosted models become a realistic procurement option for ICBs and trusts; if it is squeezed, the choice narrows permanently to a handful of American APIs. That is worth knowing when your practice or PCN next signs a scribe contract: ask where the model runs, not just where the data is stored.

items.title: A ban drafted in Washington is a supplier risk in Harrow
items.body: The concrete proposal in this edition is a US ban on Chinese open models. Several cheaper transcription and summarisation tools sold into UK primary care are built on open weights of uncertain provenance, and suppliers rarely volunteer which base model they fine-tuned. If restrictions land, some of those products change model or price at short notice — the same quiet substitution problem as any model swap, but forced by policy rather than engineering. The reasonable step is dull and cheap: ask each AI supplier, in writing, which base model the product uses, and whether they would notify you if it changed. Keep the answer with the DPIA.

items.title: The safety argument is not obviously wrong, and neither is the cynical one
items.body: Anthropic's refusal to sign rests on Dario Amodei's worry about frontier-grade cyber capability being downloadable by anyone. If he is right, a health service running on internet-facing clinical systems is exactly the sort of target that finds out first — the 2017 WannaCry week is still the reference point for most of us. If Zitron and the cynics are right, the whole exchange is commercial positioning between firms with capex to justify, and safety language is the wrapper. General practice does not need to pick. Either way the operational lesson is the same one the NHS keeps relearning: patch, segment, and rehearse the paper fallback, because your exposure comes from the estate you actually run rather than from whose model won the argument.

the_other_side.source: The More You Buy, The More You Lose
the_other_side.text: Zitron published the same day and does not engage the open-weight argument at all — no mention of the letter, of Kimi, or of Anthropic's refusal to sign. What he does contest is the premise underneath it: that these companies are large, healthy actors whose commercial interests happen to point at a public good. He takes this edition's lead headline, NVIDIA's investment in Safe Superintelligence, and files it under manufactured demand, describing SSI as "a company with no products or plans other than to rent NVIDIA GPUs", and reads the reported $250bn backstop for a SoftBank-affiliate data centre as "the final boss of circular financing". His argument is that hyperscalers cannot stop spending without being graded on what they bought, so the coordination we are watching — investments, guarantees, joint letters — is what an industry does when genuine paying demand is thinner than the capex requires.

the_truth_beneath.text: The variable both men orbit is whether coordinated corporate behaviour in AI reflects real demand or manufactured demand. Both accept the same facts — NVIDIA's $750bn of new deals, the SSI investment, and that public positions track commercial positions; NLW's own guest calls the letter eight trillion dollars of market cap acting because it is good for their business. The empirical question that will resolve is whether the backstopped capacity is built and paid for by customers rather than by guarantees, and the observable is whether SB Energy raises the debt and energises meaningful load. The residue is worldview: NLW sees self-interest converging with a public good, Zitron sees an industry that cannot find buyers. NLW is vindicated if open-weight competition and the build-out proceed on their own money; Zitron if vendor guarantees keep paying. Both are polemicists with incentives — NLW's show needs the fight to matter, Zitron's subscribers need collapse to be certain — and the signal is that both, from opposite priors, treat commercial self-interest as the honest explanation of the letter. Watch whether that site breaks ground.

headlines.headline: NVIDIA bets on Ilya's Safe Superintelligence
headlines.summary: NVIDIA made a substantial (undisclosed) investment in Ilya Sutskever's secretive SSI and granted access to its next-gen Vera Rubin chips, after gaining 'rare access' to SSI's technology. Sources say SSI had been relying on Google's TPUs.

headlines.headline: We reached the point where our research is worth scaling.
headlines.attribution: Safe Superintelligence, on the NVIDIA partnership
headlines.summary: SSI framed the NVIDIA deal as a signal of progress, saying the partnership will let it scale, and expects to 10x its compute over the next 12 months.

headlines.headline: Deep learning happens when a small cracked team operates a big computer. The computer just got bigger.
headlines.summary: SSI co-founder Daniel Levy's line captured the company's straight-shot-to-superintelligence ethos — treating short-term commercial work as a distraction from the ultimate mission.

headlines.headline: The circular AI financing chart is back
headlines.summary: NVIDIA fell 4% Monday as roughly $750B in new deals struck some as too circular — including a $500B+ partnership with SK Group and a $250B deal backstopping an OpenAI data center. Expect the circular-deal chart from last year to make a comeback.

headlines.headline: China's AI czar: resisting domestic chips makes you a traitor
headlines.summary: After a Huawei demo showed dramatic progress, Beijing pushed hard toward domestic chips, with the AI czar reportedly warning big AI users that resisting was traitorous. China's US-chip dependence fell from 90% in 2021 to 60% in 2025, and Morgan Stanley sees 25% within five years.

headlines.headline: If the US hadn't forced our industry into a corner, we never would have done something like this.
headlines.summary: Huawei Deputy Chairman Eric Xu on why China built its own chip economy. Analysts still expect China to lag the US in the chip race through at least 2030, but Huawei alone plans to ship ~1.5M AI chips this year.

headlines.headline: China's fab bottleneck is easing faster than expected
headlines.summary: Denied ASML's cutting-edge fabs, China's supply chain makes ~28,000 advanced logic chips a month — a fraction of TSMC — but Bernstein sees that doubling yearly for three years. The Information reported a Shanghai firm has begun mass-producing DUV lithography machines, tech previously kept from China.

headlines.headline: Apple vs Micron: a lobbying war over Chinese memory
headlines.summary: Apple is lobbying the White House to buy Chinese memory chips from makers like CXMT, warning of $5,000 iPhones as prices spike. Micron — the only sizable US memory maker — is lobbying to keep restrictions, warning Chinese entrants could decimate the domestic industry like steel.

headlines.headline: The open-vs-closed debate hit a new fever pitch
headlines.summary: NLW frames the open-weight fight as completely dominating the insider AI conversation — Jensen Huang's open letter drew 62 million views on his first-ever X post, a signal of just how big this has become.

headlines.headline: Chinese open models triggered a Washington freakout
headlines.summary: Concern built through GLM and then Kimi K3 — at 2.8 trillion parameters, the largest open-source model ever, beating Fable on a front-end code arena. That was enough for non-technical policymakers to move from quietly concerned to a full-on freak-out and float banning Chinese open models.

headlines.headline: Open source is not open season on American IP.
headlines.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the administration supports open source but that covert industrial-scale distillation attacks crossing into IP theft would put sanctions and entity-list designations on the table.

headlines.headline: Lutnick emerges as the pro-competition holdout
headlines.summary: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick became the lone administration official pushing competition over a ban, reportedly meeting multiple labs. His case got a boost when Kimi K3 was revealed to lag significantly behind Mythos on crucial cybersecurity benchmarks. Y Combinator's 'Little Tech Association' also pushed back, warning of a startup extinction event.

headlines.headline: Big Tech's open-weight letter lands
headlines.summary: On Friday a widely supported open letter invoked the history of open-source software, arguing US AI leadership will be judged by whether it builds a strong open ecosystem — open weights being models anyone can download, inspect, modify and run on their own infrastructure.

headlines.headline: The letter draws a line between distillation and IP theft
headlines.summary: It argued distillation — using one model's outputs to improve another — is a legitimate, long-standing technique, while unlawful extraction from closed models should be handled through targeted legal frameworks, not sweeping bans. It even claimed openness aids safety by removing single points of failure.

headlines.headline: The world needs both frontier closed models and frontier open models.
headlines.summary: Jensen Huang led the charge with his first-ever X post backing the letter, arguing open models strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate diffusion, and enable sovereignty.

headlines.headline: Sundar, Satya, Zuck and Musk all co-sign
headlines.summary: Google's Sundar Pichai (citing Gemma), Microsoft's Satya Nadella, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg ('open source is a positive and important force... preventing centralization'), and Elon Musk ('This has my full support. Jensen is right') all backed the letter alongside dozens of firms.

headlines.headline: We reject a future where a select few closed frontier models rule them all.
headlines.summary: Palantir, a onetime new entrant now standing with tech's biggest players, framed open-weight AI as essential to sovereignty, competition, and keeping customers in control.

headlines.headline: Eight trillion dollars of market cap coming out in support of open weights because it's good for their business.
headlines.summary: Packy McCormick's gleeful read: capitalism aligning corporate self-interest with consumer benefit. Others like Aravind Srinivas and Aaron Levie called it the biggest, most broad-based show of alignment tech has ever seen.

headlines.headline: OpenAI joins the letter after pushback
headlines.summary: Sam Altman initially responded warmly without signing ('I want the US to win in AI, both in open source and proprietary models'), but after significant pushback OpenAI was added as a signatory — leaving Anthropic as the sole frontier-lab holdout.

headlines.headline: The entire tech industry, save for Anthropic, has come out in favor of open source AI.
headlines.summary: Former AI czar David Sacks predicted 'the gaslighting begins' — that Anthropic won't stop until it kneecaps open source — and urged the industry to watch them like a hawk.

headlines.headline: If we get Mythos-class cyber abilities available for anyone to download... I think it's a serious concern.
headlines.summary: Anthropic's refusal to sign tracks with CEO Dario Amodei's repeated warnings about the risks of powerful open models, especially Chinese ones — comments made in a June Bloomberg interview.

headlines.headline: Geopolitics and morality are mostly just noise... they really care about losing, and they are losing.
headlines.summary: Buco Capital's cynical read: OpenAI and Anthropic are objectively kicking everyone's butt on revenue, and the coalition is scared rivals talking their book. The open letter, they argued, suggests the two labs are doing even better than thought.

headlines.headline: Are we going to head to a world of AI authoritarianism or liberty?
headlines.summary: Sam Altman's framing suggests OpenAI's support isn't purely reputational — his stated fear of a small number of companies controlling AI intersects with the open-weight case.

headlines.headline: Anthropic's holdout earns it 'aura'
headlines.summary: Several commentators praised Anthropic for standing on principle rather than signing and lobbying quietly. Signal noted that if an open-weight model is ever involved in a serious security incident, Anthropic's position 'will look a lot more prescient' — the nature of a principled stance.

headlines.headline: Anthropic staffer's snark backfires
headlines.summary: Anthropic technical-staff member Julian Schrittwieser mocked the coalition ('Can't wait for the open sourcing of Windows and MS Office'), drawing aghast responses. Bill Gurley, Matthew Berman and A16Z's Justine Moore piled on — Moore quipping about adding 'aura loss from employee tweets' to Anthropic's S-1 risk section.

headlines.headline: There is no way to hold a consistent belief set where you're AGI-pilled and pro open source.
headlines.summary: OpenAI's Rune argued the two positions are incompatible; Ethan Mollick countered that most open-weight advocates simply don't share lab insiders' belief in grave semi-autonomous AI risks — and therefore suspect the labs of spreading FUD to protect margins via regulation.
